CausalChain: Metabolic stress in cancer cells -> Decreased NSUN2 activity resulting in reduced m5C modification of tRNAs -> Increased susceptibility of tRNAs to cleavage by angiogenin -> Accumulation of specific tRFs -> tRFs modulate translation by displacing initiation factors and promoting ribosome biogenesis -> Selective translation of survival and metabolic adaptation genes -> Enhanced tumor cell survival under metabolic stress
Hypothesis: A subset of tRNA-derived fragments generated due to stress-induced loss of tRNA methylation (e.g., m5C) acts as a molecular switch to reprogram the translational machinery in cancer cells, thereby promoting survival and metabolic adaptation under conditions of metabolic stress.
Abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that tRNA‐derived fragments (tRFs) not only serve as regulators of gene expression through miRNA‐like and RNA‐binding protein displacement mechanisms but may also function as key modulators of translational reprogramming under metabolic stress. In this hypothesis, we propose that in cancer cells, metabolic stress leads to altered tRNA epitranscriptomic modifications – specifically, a reduction in cytosine‐5 methylation (m5C) mediated by enzymes such as NSUN2. This loss of modification renders tRNAs more susceptible to endonucleolytic cleavage by angiogenin, resulting in the accumulation of a distinct subset of tRFs. These stress‐induced tRFs, in turn, remodel the protein synthesis machinery by displacing translation initiation factors and promoting ribosome biogenesis, thereby selectively enhancing the translation of survival and metabolic adaptation genes. Our hypothesis posits that this dynamic switch in the translational landscape supports tumor cell survival under adverse metabolic conditions and offers a novel target for therapeutic intervention.
